The stranger whose name was I cbaldo, became enamoured of the daughter of an ancient house, nlrendv affianced to another. He demanded her hand in marriage and was of course rejected. Enraged at this ho studied how to lie revenged. Profoundly skilled in the mechanical arts, he allowed himself no rest until he had invented the most formidable weapon which could be imagined. This was a key of large size, the handle of | which was so constructed that it could he j turned round with little difficulty. W hen j turned it discovered a spring which on pressure, launched from the other end a needle of I lancet of such subtile fineness that it entered regretted that the acts of indiscreet people I into the flesh and buried itself there without should lead to results injurious to the welfare 1 leaving external trace. lebaldo waited in j disguise, at the door ol the church in which the maiden he loved was about to receive the þÿ nuptial benediction. '1 he assassin sent the slender steel unperceived, into the breast of the bridegroom. þÿ lie I wounded man had no suspicion injury ol , but seized with sudden and sharp pain in the midst of the ceremony,

he fainted, and was carried to his house amid the lamentations of the bridal party. am was all the skill of the physicians, who could not divine the cause of this strange illness, and in a few days he died. Tebaldo again demanded the hand of the maiden from her parents, and received the second refusal. They too perished miserably in a few days. The face of the foreigner had been j ever displeasing to her, but since the death of all those most dear to her if had become odious (as though she had a presentiment of his guilt) and her reply was most decisive in the negative. Tebaldo, beyond himself with rage, attempted to wound her through the gate and succeeded ; the secrecy of the place prevented his movement from being observed. On her return to her room the maiden felt a pain in her breast and uncovering it she found il spotted w ith a single drop of blood. From the New Orleans True American, May 31- Imporlant from Mexico. þÿ \ friend who arrived yesterday from Vera Cruz and Tampico, has furnished us with the following information. Col. Bee, minister of Texas to Mexico had arrived at Vera Cruz, and applied to Gen. Victoria, then in command, for permission to land, which the General refused to grant, on pain of immediate imprisonment. The Colonel was informed that fie might stay on board of anv vessel in the harbor Colonel Bee replied that if he could not land, he would be compelled to throw himself on the hospitality of the French commander then at Sacrifieios, which he accordingly did, and was received with marked attention and distinction ; but before he could remove his effects to the French þÿcommander s ship he received a passport from Gen. V. granting him permission to remain at Vera Cruz until he could heat from the supreme government. Colonel B. accepted the passport and permission, and landed. The city of Tampico was besieged by the government troops under Bustamente, who was at Altemira, twenty miles distant. His cavalry had advanced within a quarter of a mile of Tampico, drove in the pickets, after capturing 10 or 12 men. The only troops in Tampico were the militia of the town. Gen. Urrea had arrived and was expected to be joined by 300 men, the remnant of those who bad escaped after the conflict near Puebla under Mexia. If they should arrive in time, the force will be increased to 1000. The city was strongly fortified, and it is pro-

bable that from the temper displayed by the people they will make a most obstinate j defence. There was lying off the port of Tampico the U. S. ship Warren, the Br. sloop of war Cotnus, and a French gun brig. 'The best understanding prevailed among the officers of the different vessels for the mutual protection of the foreign interests, and no doubt every thing in their power will be done to render assistance, but as the vessels themselves are lying nine miles from the city, with a very bad bat between it and them, it is feared that when the critical moment shall arrive, requiring their assistance, they will be unable to render >t. The general opinion among the best informed people is, that upon the fall ol Tampico, Santa Anna will be declared Director, and that his plan is to close all the Mexican ports against foreign commerce, with the exception ol Vera Cruz,

LATEST FROM MEXICO. From Vera Cruz, we learn that the Texian minister to Mexico, was received with gross insults, and not allowed to proceed to the capital. From the capital, we learn that General Urrea has been taken and carried there wounded. Santa Anna was received with the most extravagant demonstrations of joy. It is said in the papers that he is taking the most active measures to recruit soldiers, and till up the army skeletons. An official report gives the number authorized by law, viz: þÿ 9,t>0l) cavalry, 3000 artillery, and 20,000 infantry. It appears that the number actually under arms is little over one third of the force called for law, say 2,800 artillery, 3000 cavalry, and about 8000 infantry.

ARRIVAL OF AN IRON STEAMBOAT. The N. York Evening Post says: þÿ An experimental steamboat, built to run on the Delaware and Raritan Canal, has just arrived in New York, from London, after a passage of foity-five days. The name of the vessel is the Robert L. Stockton, an iron schooner, fitted with Captain þÿErieson s patent engine, and commanded by Captain John R. Crane, an intrepid and skilful seaman. She came out under canvass, without the aid of steam. Her departure from London was looked upon as an act of great temerity in Captain Crane, whose success, however, has fully justified his reliance on his own skill and the capacity of his vessel to brave the storms of the Atlantic. The Stockton is, we believe, the fist vessel of this kind, ever seen in America. She is built entirely of iron, the pieces being rivetted together, is rated fifteen tons, and is seventy one feet long, while her breadth at midships is only ten feet. It was this disproportion which caused the voyage to be considered so hazardous. The steam engine is placed at the stern, which Captain Crane considers an advantageous mode of construction in steamboats intended for the open þÿsea. þÿ Ibid June 2fi.

St. Croix Ciiiiistiansted (Monday) 8th July, 1839. By the first June p icket from England tee learn that Parliament met on the 27 tli of May and proceeded to the choice of a Speaker of the House of Commons in place of Mr. Abercromhy resigned, and who has been created a Peer under the title of Lord Dumfernhne. Both parties mustered their full strength, and the result was as follows þÿ for Mr. Shaw Lefevre, the ministerial candidate, 317 Mr. Goulbourue, the conservative candidate, 299

majority 18 and Mr Lefevre was declared elected and took the chair. The Bill to suspend the constitution of Jamaica has been abandoned by ministers , and a new one (less obnoxious), introduced by Mr, Labouchere. A Bill to establish Normal Schools and to promote National education, has greatly excited the ire of the high dignitaries of the church oj England and of the high church party þÿ the cause of the antipathy to the bill appears to be, that these schools are not to be placed exclusively under the control of the established church, and are intended to be foi the benefit of all denominations ; hie bill is a favorite measuie of Lord John Bussell, and was to be taken up on the 1 Ith of June, but from the powerful hostility it has excited., it is supposed that he will be left in a minority. A Bill relating to the Government of Canada was to be shortly introduced, and it is also thought it would meet with great opposition. þÿ In the house of Lords, Lord H harnclijfe call'd upon Lord Melbourne for explanation of his reasons for re-accepting his place, otter having declared he could not advantageously administer the Government under the present powerful opposition. Lord A1 replied that he had already explained, and he declared that no sacrifice of principles were involved in said to office ; the Duke of Wellington his return that he never saw sufficient reason for the resignation of ministers, and justified them in continuing to administer the Government. The Queen's birth day was celebrated on the

18</t May with much splendour. Bell's weekly messenger of 25 th May observes however that in passing from Buckingham palace to St. James', her Majesty was not greeted with the usual cheers from the populace, but that n respectful silence was observed, and that the Duke of Wellington was most heartily cheered, and Lord Melbourne hissed and hooted in going to and returning from the. palace. The Dowager Queen of England had returned home, in the Hastings 71. The Crown Bn nee and Grand Duke Alexander of Russia had been received in London with great attention þÿ balls, reviews, dinners <jjc , rapidly succeeded each other. The Grand Duke had made many munificent prctents for charitable purposes, and had given 600 £ Stlg. in aid of the monuments erecting in London in honor of Wellington and Nelson. The papers announce, the decease of the exqueen of Naples, sister to Napoleon aged 58 ; she died of the same, complaint as her bi other, a Cancer of the stomach The decease of Cardinal Fesch ( uncle to Napoleon) at Rome is also announced, he died immensely rich. Every tiling was tranquil at Baris, and Louis Philippe is said to have become, more popular since the. late insurrection, particularly with the military Marshal Soult, who is approaching his 80 th year, it is said., will soon retire from public life. Many arrests had been made at Baris, and it was ascertained that the insurrectionists were among the lowest of the population oj the fauxbourgs, St. Alai tin and St. Antoine.

The arrival of her Britannic þÿMajesty brig s Buzzard, bringing with her the Spanish brig Eagle as a prize, has been considered somewhat mysterious, and some of our contemporaries have naturally enough expressed their doubts as to the accuracy of the accounts furnished by the ship news collectors. That a Spanish slaver should have been captured by a British cruiser as a slave vessel, and brought to this port as a prize, was certainly a little extraordinary, but Mr. Buchanan, the British Consul, has explained it to us in such a manner as to remove all mystery. Her Majesty's brig Buzzard captured the Eagle on the coast of Africa þÿ probably the first time the Eagle ever quailed to the Buzzard þÿ together with another vessel as slave traders. They were both under American colors, manned with Spaniards from Havana and commanded by Americans ; both of them had the irons necessary for securing slaves and were in all respects fitted lor the horrid tralfie on the coast; indeed the crews confessed to the officers of the Buzzard that the vessels were on a visit to the African coast expressly tor the purpose of obtaining slaves, and added that they would have secured a cargo, but tor the interference of that vessel. 1 he slaves were carried into Barbados but were sent to the United States through a friendly feeling on the part of the British authorities towards the people of the U. States. They were yesterdav handed over by the Consul, to the U. S. Marshal to be dealt with as our authorities

think proper. This must certainly be con sidered a very handsome act of the British authorities, and one that evinces very empha tically the disposition felt by the Government of Great Britain and every one in authority under it, to treat the American Government and people in the friendliest spirit. We hope the feeling will be reciprocated as it ought to be, and we hope further that the miscreants who have attempted the worst species of piracy þÿ that of stealing slaves þÿ under our flag, may be punished to the utmost limit of the law.

ATIIS. - Jtmumtn Military Bridges. þÿ It has very frequently happened during great military operations that the passage of rivers by bodies ol troops has been found impassable, at a moment when it would have led to the most important results, owing to the roads leading up to their banks being unfit for wheel carriages over the points where it lias been desired to cross. The carriages now in use for the pontoons or portable boats generally employed in constructing temporary military bridges are necessarily so large, and so heavy and cumbersome when loaded, as to require as many as eight or 10 horses to each carriage, unless on the smoothest roads, and may be seen and beard from such a distance as to make it impossible to perform any movement with them concealed from an enemy watching, as is usual, the principal roads leading to rivers in its vicinity. On Monday morning an experiment was made by Col Macintosh on the Serpentine river, in presence of the Duke of Wellington, Lord Hill, the General Commanding in Chief, General Sir J. Macdonald Sir J. Gardiner, and many other distinguished officers, which holds out the promise of the complete attainment of the object in view. Two pontoons composed of every portable materials, supporting a wooden platform (and although constituting only a small portion of a bridge, sufficient to judge of results from), had been placed upon the water, forty men of the foot Guards were diiected to occupy it. Their weight may be calculated at

about a ton, more that of a peice ol heavy ordinance, but. as the pontoons were not immersed to quite half their depth, it is obvious that they could have supported a much greater weight. The raft then formed was towed out to some distance in the Serpentine. It sailed admirably and the men appeared to be at pei feet ease in it, for, by the command of the Duke of Wellington, the soldiers first stood up, then sat down, and finally laid down. After the curiosity of the different witnesses had been sufficiently gratified, the raft was towed to shore, and the planks being removed, the vessels which Lad sustained them, and which were composed of a preparation of India llubher, and inflated with airt were deprived of the air anil the weight of each was ihen not more than one horse was fully capable of carrying. From eight to twelve of these vessels would form a bridge of sufficient length to cross most of the rontimontal rivers. Another experiment followed which was as important in its nature as the preceding. This vessel was also formed of India Rubber, and presented the appearance of a great ball, with couple of legs attached to the bottom and the top cut off. It was set floating on the river, and a man, by means of a boat, got into it ; his legs went into the places assigned them, and the bar enclosed the major part of his body, the logs and part of the other lay under water. The man having provided himself w ith two small paddles, then proceeded to work his way into

the river, at the same time keeping his legs in active motion. Having reached the middle with great care, he waded back, and landed in the midst of enthusiastic cheers. The object of this invention is to enable a man to >ord a liver, and at die same time convey a rope, or something of a like nature, from one shore to the other. þÿ Naval and Military Gazette. þÿ þÿ þÿ -TSZJWL G-Vgt þÿ Printed and Published by lUCh ALU JU'ICLL'IT,

return, the Austrian Ambassador was waiting to have an interview with Louis Philippe which lasted from seven until nine o'clock and not until the latter hour was his Majesty

A delicious odour emanates from the leaves and | berries; and the wax or resin proceeding from these latter, spreads around the same j perfume, when burning ; so that a single taper is sufficient to perfume a good sized room, even for some time after it has been extinguished. We are decidedly of opinion, that the climate of England would be perfectly I suitable for the cultivation of this plant, and J we are equally convinced, that it w'ould con- j fer a great value on lands now unproductive. The Nantucket Inquirer publishes the following article from a London periodical of 1783, as corroborative evidence of an often asserted fact, that the first vessel which displayed our National flag on the waters of Great Britain, was a Nantucket ship: The Thirteen Stripes. The ship Bedford, Captain Moores, belonging to Massachusetts, arrived iii the Downs the 3d of February, passed Gravesend the 4th, and was reported at the custom house the 0th instant, Slie w as not allowed regular entry until some consultation had taken place between the commissioners of the customs and the lords of council, on account of the many acts of parliament yet in force against the rebels in America. She is loaded with 487 butts of whale oil, is American built, manned wholly by A me i ican seamen, wears the rebel colors, and belongs to the island of Nantucket, in Massachusetts. This is the first vessel which displayed the thirteen rebellious stripes of America in any British port. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, May 13. THE BOUNDARY QUESTION. From the Globe. Special Mission to England.

The President has determined not to send a special minister to England at present, and we are permitted to publish the following extracts from the correspondence between Lord Palmerston and Mr. Stevenson, as explanatory of the views of -the two governments upon the subject.

EXTRACT MR. ST1VENSON TO LORD PALMERSTON. Lord Palmerston has probably already been apprised that, among the proceedings of the Congress of the United States at the close of its last session, provision wai made for a special mission to Great Britain, in relation to the subject of this controversy, should it, in the opinion of the President, be deemed advisable to appoint one. In virtue of this provision, the undersigned has now the honor of acquainting his Lordship that the President of the United States (desirous of conforming to the indicated wishes of Congress) has directed him to announce to her þÿMajesty gov- s ernment his willingness to institute such a mission, and change the place of negociation, which had heretofore been agreed on, from Washington to London; provided it should be agreeable to her þÿMajesty sgovernment to do so, and would, in their opinion, be the means oi hastening or facilitating the linal adjustment of the controversy. In submitting this proposition of the President, which he has now the honor of doing, the undersigned flatters himself that Lord Palmerston will not fail to appreciate the motives which have influenced the President in making it, and see in it, notonlv an additional proof of his desire to terminate amicably this protracted and paiulul controversy, but the earnest solicitude which he feels to place the relations of the two countries beyond the reach of those casualties by which, in the present state of things, they are so liable to be

injured. To this proposition, tbe undersigned has been directed respectfully to urge the early consideration of her þÿMajesty government. s The importance and urgency of bringing to a speedy close the pending negotiation, and the existing embarrassments in which the two countries are now placed, will, the undersigned persuades himself, sufficiently explain the earnestness with which he has pressed the subject upon the consideration of Lord Palmerston; and, in closing this note, he can but indulge the confident hope that the final determination of her þÿMajesty government s will not only correspond with the just expectations which are entertained by his own government, bnt that it will be the means of leading to such an adjustment of the whole controversy as may be compatible with the just rights and honor of the two countries, and the peaceful and friendly relations, upon the preservation of which so essentially depend the prosperity and happiness of both. (Signed) A STEVENSON. 23 Portland place, March 30, 1839.
Extract LORD PALMERSTON TO MR. STEVENSON. Her þÿMajesty sgovernment consider the communication which Mr. Stevenson lias been instructed to make to the undersigned

A'?I3 upon the subject of the proposed mission of a special envoy to England as a fresh proof of the friendly disposition of the President, and of the frankness which it is hoped will always characterize the intercourse between the two governments, and her þÿMajesty government s hastens to reply to that communication in the same spirit and with the same þÿfrankness. The President is desirous of knowing whether such a mission would be agreeable to her Majesty's government, and whether it would, in their opinion, be the means of hastening or facilitating the final adjustment of the controversy. That it would always be agreeable to her þÿMajesty s government to receive any person enjoying the confidence of the President, and sent hither to treat of matters affecting the interests of both countries, the undersigned is persuaded that the government of the United States cannot possibly doubt ; but her þÿMajesty government s do not see that in the present state of the negotiations such a mission could be likely to hasten or to facilitate the adjustment of the controversy. It was the wish of the British government in 1831, when the award of the King of the Netherlands was given, that any farther negotiation which might be necessary upon this subject, would be carried on in London. But the government of the United States expressed a strong desire that the seat of negotiation should be in Washington, and the British government acquiesced in that arrangement. Now the question at present to be consider-

ed is whether any advantages , would arise from transferring the negotiation to London. Undoubtedly if the state of the negotiation were such that the two governments were at liberty to arrive at a final and immediate settlement of the controversy by a conventional division of the territory in dispute, her Majesty's government would be of opinion that advantage might arise from the mission proposed to be sent to this country by the government of the United States. But Maine having refused to agree to a conventional line, and another reference to arbitration being in the present slate of the matter out of the question ; the only course left upon for the two governments, with a view to arrive at a solution of the controversy, is to cause a fresh survey of the territory to be made, for the purpose of endeavoring to trace upon the ground itself, the line of the treaty of 1783 ; and the undersigned is sending to Mr. Fox, for the consideration of the President, a draft of a convention for the purpose of regulating the proceedings of the two commissioners to be appointed by the two governments for this end ; and her þÿMajesty government s hope that the report of these commissioners will either settle the question at issue, or furnish to the two governments such information as may lead directly to a settlement. But this being the present state of the matter, it appears to her þÿMajesty Government s that a special envoy now sent from America, would not, upon his arrival in this country,

find any thing to discuss or settle in connection with this question, the discussion or settlement of which could be of importance commensurate with the expectations which such a mission would naturally excite on both sides of the Atlantic ; and that if, in consequence thereof, the envoy so sent were to return to the United States before the two governments had finally settled the whole question, a disappointment might thereby be j cieated, which, however unfounded it might | be, might, nevertheless, produce bad effects in both countries.

From Ike St. James's Chronicle, April 30. " Paris, April HI. " It was said to-day, in the Salle des Conferences, that the Marshal Souit declared his mission to be terminated. It was not said that he had returned into the hands ol the Boglioldcr ' King the powers entrusted to him. " At half past three, Messrs. Dnpin and Passy were called to the Palace. The Centre Gauche ministry is all formed, and at the disposal of the King. If it be not in the Monitcnr of tomorrow or the next day, it vvilj only be because the King has not accepted " the proposal Yesterd iv the King sent for M. Passy, as President of the Chamber of Deputies. On arriving at the Tuilleries he was prepared with his list of Centre Gauche ministry to submit to the King. The name of Marshal Soult was placed at the head as Minister of War and President of the Council. But in the event of Marshal Soult refusing to accept this post, then Admiral Dupcri e was proposed as his substitute. The King, supposing that 1/ Passy was aware that the marshal had resigned his powers the night before, said nothing on the subject, but entreated H. Passy to see the marshal and endeavour to persuade him to accept the post of President. M. P assy proposed that the programme should lie the same as that drawn up by M. Thiers on the 81st March þÿ text and commentary. At half past four 1/. Dupin arrived at the Palace, having been sent for by his Majesty. He came with the same identical list as M. Passv, and had precisely the same reasons

to give, and exactly the same programme. Although the King desired a much more Conservative Cabinet, yet he expressed no intention to oppose the formation of a ministrv, provided Marshal Sonlt would consent to head it. His Majesty then requested M" Dupin also to sec the marshal, and endeavour to prevail on him to accept office. In the evening M. Passy, but not M. Dttpiti returned to the King. lie expressed his surprise that the resignation of Marshal Soult on the previous night had not been mentioned cither to himself, M. Dttpin, or M. Teste ; but the King was surprised that the three honourable deputies were not aware of the circumstance, as it had not been kept a secret. The King expressed much chagrin and great annoyance that Marshal Soult should refuse to accept the post of President of the Council, and stated that lie would himself make one m«»re effort to prevail on him to change his mind. He directed, however, M. Pnsy to return to the Palace to day, and to receive his determination. Last night it is said, h s Majesty wrote to the marshal an urgent 1(9ter, but it is not thought that he will consent to enter a ministry of which M. Thiers shall be Minister of Foreign Aliairs, without H,

Guizot or Duchatel being counteracting or counterbalancing members. Their entry is quite out of the question with the Centre Gauche. liut to-morrow is the fatal day. If the Moniteur of to-morrow shall not contain the ministry, the address to the King will be persevered in, and a new order of events will begin here. The Coarrier Francais counsels the members of the Chamber of Deputies to refuse to examine the budget until a ministry shall be named. The Sjecle goes further, and says that many deputies have retused to examine the budget in the bureau.

news fko:,t spaln- The following telegraphic dispatch from Bayonne is not without importance : þÿ " Bayonne, April 25, half past one. " The couriers w ho w- re behind hand from Madrid have arrived. The division of Para has re-established the communications. 'I he General Nogueras is named to the command of the army of the centre in place of Van Haleu." This dispatch relates to the communications by the route from Saragossa, which, Cabrera intercepted from the time of the check of General Van Ilalen before Segura. This general has been turned out of his post for his failure, as were his predecessors Orua and San Miguel. This is the third generalin chief of the army of the centre who has failed against Cabrera. The government of Madrid has enough to do now to reinforce the army of the Queen in Lower Arragon.

The line of telegraph between St. Petersburgh and Warsaw has just been completed. On the 12th inst. the first telegraphic dispatch was received in Berlin, announcing that the Empress had been seriously indisposed, but was quite recovered. News can now be received in Berlin front St. Petersburg!) in four days. The Leipsie inhabitants are rejoicing at the great commercial prospect before tliern by the opening of the railroad. They expect that they will rival shortly Hamburgh and Frankfort in the extent of their mercantile transactions.

SILK CULTURE. Gay's Machine. Silk is going ahead. The signs are more favorable for the cultivation of this new staple, than they were when the South began to turn her attention toward the growth of cotton. The Moras Multicauhs, which grows with such rapidity that it furnishes food for the worm, in the very Spring when it is planted, furnishes one essential link towards its production. The invention of new machines, for reeling and manufacturing the silk into various forms, enables the planter to turn his cocoons at once to account. The weakest part of our slave population, the \oung and the old, may be piolilably employ-

. «Ma Jtrf ' «. 'MMh l. . .-» »» ' ed þÿ and as we heard a Virginian Tobacco Planter declare the other evening, it would not he astonishing, if Gay's Machine were to eflect a singular revolution in Virginia, by keeping many of our people at home, who would otherwise have gone to the coltou regions of the South and South west þÿ and by bringing more population and capital to our Slate, and llitis creating a new and important element of her prosperity. We allude to Clay's Machinery , which has been exhibited for some days past in this city. By the turning of a wheel, which any child can do, cocoons are wound off, and converted at once into the most beautiful silk for the needle or loom. All who have seen it, have been struck with the ease, regularity and result of its operation, and ihe mechanical genius of its inventor A view of (he process appears to have inspired all with the same impression, that now we can make our own silk, and that we must no longer pay a tax of twenty millions for a commodity which every circumstance and facility invites us to make for ourselves. We understand, that Mr Gay has disposed of the Patent right in several Suites. New Jersey, for example, at $15,000 þÿ and the Company which purchased the right, cleared at once $15,000 bv the speculation. He asks $30,000 for Virginia þÿ and at Norfolk alone, about $10 000 were taken. Several shares have already been taken in ibis city.

COLONI A B NEWS. The brigamine Eagle, Baltimore built, arrived here on Tuesday last from Princes Island (African Coast) in charge of part of the crew of her Majesty's brigantine Buzzard. The Eagle has accommodation for the conveyance of slaves. The Eagle was taken by the Buzzard off Fernando Po on the 13th March, under American colours and with false papers. The Buzzard arrived on Sunday last liom Princes Island, having captured another slaver called the Clara, which vessel has since arrived. þÿ West Indian, May 20.

H. M. Brigantine Buzzard, Lieut. Fitzgerald, sailed for New York, yesterday morning. having under eseort the two prizes, Eagle and Clara, captured on the Afrrioaii coast. These two vessels being American built, are taken to New York for condemnation, should they be acknowledged by their government, if not, they will be taken back to Sierra Leone, and there condemned. This is the third slaver taken within the space of a few months by the active and vigilant commander of the Buzzard. þÿ ibid, Way 'c3.

SPAIN. We have received the Madrid journals to the 20tli instant inclusive. The road to France had been completely intercepted during three days by a column of Cabrera's army, commanded by bis two Lieutenants Polo and Marc.ottel. The latter, alter fortifying lite villages of Asustante and Fueiite do

a» tt«W n+r. Snz, proceeded witli n portion of his men to Trillo, to the right of the Tagus. The inhabitants every where abandoned their houses on his approach The town of Brihuega was completely deserted, and the fugitives were pursued to the very gates of Guadalaxara by the Carlist detachments. In the mean lime, another party, about 30(10 strong, invested the fort of Aleotea, which being abandoned to itself could not long hold out. The fort of Cifuentes was menaced with the same danger, it being Cabrera's plan to seize on all t he forts of Lower Arragon, in order to extend his domination as lar as the gates of Madrid. Van Ilalen is to he tried by a court martial for abandoning Segura. The public loudly murmured against General Espartero for his want of energy, and his inbability to achieve any feat with the imposing force placed under his orders. The critical situation of affairs naturally excited much uneasiness in the money-market, and the funds evinced a tendency to decline. Only one cash transaction was done in the Five per Cents oil the 20th, at liD.

MISCELLANEOUS. The Augsberg Gazelle contains a letter from Vienna of the 4th inst., stating that M. Zea Bermudez had not been well received by the Austrian Cabinet. Prince Metternicli only granted him one audience, at which lie was staled to have told the Spanish diplomatist that bis departure from Vienna would be agreeable to the government. He was, accordingly. to leave Vienna on the 5lh The same letter mentions that the latest intelligence from Constantinople wag ot an alarming character. The Sultan was anxious for war, and actively preparing for it. " Letters from Constantinople of the 5th instant, received by express, announce that a courier from the Governor of Baynzid hud brought intelligence that the Persian army, between 40,000 and 50,000 strong, besides the Curds, with whom the Shah had entered into treaty, was about to commence its march at the end of the preceding month, notwithstanding several of the King's cottncellors had endeavoured to deter him from this new expedition. It is not said whether Herat is the object in view. Some doubts having been entertained respecting tht! intended journey to this country of the Grand Duke Alexander, eldest son of bis Majesty the Emperor of Russia, we can now slate positively that advices have been received by the Dutch mail, that his Imperial Highness, accompanied by the Prince Frederie Henry, second son of the Prince of Orange, and a numerous suite, will embark on Thursday next at Rotterdam for London, on board the Dutch government steamer the Cerberus.

"EARTH to EARTH <$- DUST to DUST." By the Rev. George Croly, L. L. D. " Earth to earth, and dust to dust !" Here the evil and the just, Here the youthful and the old, Here the fearful and the bold, Here the matron and the maid, in one silent bed are laid; Here the vassal and the king, Side by side, lie withering ; Here the sword and sceptre rust : " Earth to earth, and dust to dust!"

Age on age shall roll along O'er this pale and mighty throng : Those that wept them, those that weep, All shall with these sleepers sleep, Brothers, sisters of the worm ! Summer's sun, and winter's storm, Song of peace or battle's roar, Ne'er shall break their slumbers more : Death shall keep his silent trust, " Earth to earth, and dust to dust !"

But a day is coming fast, þÿ Earth, thv mightiest and thy last ; It shall come in tear and wonder, Heralded by trump and thunder ; It shall come in strife and toil. It shall come in blood and spoil, It shall come in empire's groans, Burning temples, trampled thrones ; Then, ambition, rue thv lust ! " Earth to earth, and dust to dust."

Then shall come the judgment sign ; In the east the king shall shine, Flashing from heaven's golden gate, Thousands, thousands, round his state, Spirits with the crown and plume : Tremble, then, thou sullen tomb, Heaven shall open on our sight, Earth be burn'd to living light, Kingdoms of the ransom'd just, þÿ " Earth to earth, and dust to dust-"

Then, shall, gorgeous as a gem, Shine thy mount Jerusalem ; Then shall in the desert rise Fruits of more than paradise ; Earth by angel-feel be trod, One great garden of her God ; Till are dried the martyr's tears Through a glorious thousand years, Now in hope of him we trust, " Earth to earth, and dust to dust."

THE TO US EES MOIS PLANT. To the Editor of the Royal Gazette and Jamaica Times. Sir, In looking over the advertisements of the London Times of a late date, I observed the following : þÿ " Tous les Mois, or Canna coccinea. A new and delicious aliment, recently introduced from the West Indies, and highly recommended, by Drs. Rvan and James Johnson, as a diet for invalids and children, on account of its lightness, nutritious quality and indisposition to acidity, being supeiior to sago, tapioca, arrow root, or gruel." Can you give me any description of, or information respecting the plant from which this aliment is made ? Does the Canna coccinea grow in Jamaica ? The only plant which resembles it in name, is the Canna Indica or Indian Shot ; but 1 do not think it will produce a " delicious aliment." The trivial French name, " Tons les Hois." is somewhat applicable to the Indian Shot, as it is in blossom nearly all the year.

Your attention to the above, at your leisure, will oblige, A Subscriber to the Roy. Gaz. February 20, 1839. In reference to the above communication, we are enabled to give the following information : þÿ There are two species of Canna (C. Indica C. coccinea), which are very common in this Island and known in common by the name of Indian Shot, and which, as they resemble one another very closely, constitute probably but one species A variety common in Peru, and from the roots of which an alimentary substance is procured, has received from Botanists the name C. edulis. The roots of the Indian Shot are about the thickness of the Sugar Cane, and are spongy and jointed. As the plant belongs to the same natural family as the arrow root (Maranta) we have a right to expect that a starch might be prepared from the root. We recollect several years ago that a premium was awarded bv the Jamaica Society to Mr. Arbourn, at that time residing in the St. Andrew's mountains, for a sample of starch procured from the root of this plant. It was found to be very palatable and was much approved of. Of late years it has been imported, under the name of Toulemons (a corruption of Tous les Alois so called from the plant flowering every month) into England, from the French Islands. Dr. Jaines Johnson in a late number of the Afedico-Chirurgical Review states that he considers it much superior to arrow root satzo, or any of the alimentary farinaceous or mucilageeus substances hitherto in use. We hope that as the Indian shot is a common and

indeed troublesome weed very difficult to eradicate in many parts of the Island, the attention of our small settlers may be called to the manufacture ot this article of food, and that we may soon have a supply in town; so that a trial ol its qualities may be made by our medical friends.

Extracts from the St. James's Chronicle, to the 13th April. PARIS, April 6. THE CllAMBElt OF DEPUTIES AND THE ROYALTY. We are arriving rapidly at a deplorable crisis. The Courier Erancais contains the following remarkable lines: þÿ - " Let the deputies make haste. The country is waiting for their decision. Three or four days will suffice for the verification des pouvoirs, and it is now time to get to a decision The Throne, apprised of public opinion has deferred to the Chambers, leaving it the exercise of a certain dictatorship. There has been no King's speech at the opening of the Chambers þÿ no programme for the session þÿ no Cabinet. The right of initative, the preponderance, the power þÿ all are placed in the hands of the Chamber. The circumstances in which it is placed give to it, as in 1830, nothing less than the power of providing tor the safety of the state." And then it adds þÿ " The mob assemble around the Chamber in which the deputies hold their sittings, waiting, as it were, for the formation of a o government by J the Chamber."

We have received the Paris journals of Thursday. Marshal Soult, it is said, still entertains a hope of forming a permanent ministry. He has been, however, for the present unsuccessful in his application to the party of M. Guizot (Doctrinaires) and to the party of M. Thiers (Centre Gauche) ; neither would comply with the Marshal's terms, though neither gave an unqualified refusal. The Chamber is chiefly occupied with election scrutinies. þÿ St. James's Chronicle April 13.
We understand that it is the intention of government to send a fleet very shortly to the Baltic, under the command of a Flag Oflicer. þÿ Ibid.

HEWS FROM SPAIN. Madrid journals and letters of the 31st ult. have come to hand, Their contents, however, are totally void of interest. The procession of the holy week had attracted, in Seville, upwards of 30,000 strangers. Seats to see them pass had fetched as high as three ounces of gold. Letters from Bayonne of the 4th instant state, that new arrests had been ordered bv General Marotto ; Generals Sopelana anil Arroyo, who had declared against him on receiptof the decree of Don Carlos of the 21st of February last, had been deprived of their commands, and were awaiting their trial, or execution, in the prison of Durango. Numbers of refugees continued to arrive daily on the French frontier, particularly from Navarre. The 5th battalion of that province had been reduced by desertion to a mere skeleton. The Carlist exiles placed their sole hope in Cabrera, with whom they were endeavouring to open a correspondence. The ex-Ministers Arias Tejeiro, Labendero, and Diego Miguel Garcia, had retired to Toulouse , others had proceeded to the department of the Eastern Pyrenees. The

Carlist chief Taiagunl was not allowed to remain in Pau. On his arrival in that city the prefect told him that he had been instructed to send him into the interior of France, and gave him a passport for Perigueux M. Gclos, the surgeon of Don Carlos, and a few other exiles, had been authorised to reside in Bayonne It was reported on the frontier that General Espartero intended to d rect a simultaneous attack against the lines ot Fstella and Remales. The concentration ot the Carlist forces on the last point paralyzed the movements of the Christine generals, arid intercepted their cornmunicatien with Santander.

SPANISH AFFAIRS. I have been favoured with the inspection of a letter written hv an oflicer of rank and merit at the head quarters of Don Carlos. þÿ That letter is full of important and valuable facts. It appeals that Don Carlos has taken a resolution which is of vast importance, and to which he has been driven by the advice and counsel of foreign powers. It is this þÿ to march into Castile, and no longer to conline the war to the Basque provinces and Navarre. The Princess de Beira was long since in favor of this measure, and she has at last conquered the repugnance of Don Carlos. The period when this onward movement will be made has not vet been fixed, hut in less than a month, i. e towards the close of April. Marotto and Cabrera are said to be converted to this opinion. A large army of occupation will he left in the Basque provinces, hut a much larger will invade Castile. It has cost Don Carlos much to come to this determination, hut it is said that he is now fully resolved, and that all the necessary measures will he promptly taken. The inhabitants of the Basque provinces begin to he wearied of the conflict, and especially of th ir provinces being always the seat of the war: a diversion in this respect cannot, then, fail of doing good. Marotto is busily engaged in re-organising Jus army, and a gieat many officers who were laid on the shelf have been recalled. Letters from Bayonne of the 31st ult state that upwards of 20,000 Christinos, provided with a numerous field and siege artillery,

were then moving from Pampeluna and Lodosa towards Sexcan and the Carlist lines of Estella. Marotto, on the other hand, was at the head of 10 battalions, hut the apostolicals in Bayonne did not anticipate any rencontre between the belligerents. They openly declared that all this marching and countermarching on both sides had been concerted between the two generals to amuse the people, and that they had no serious intention of coming to blows. The condition of the provinces was fast improving, and public opinion was daily becoming more favorable to General Marotto. It is not true that any executions had recently taken place. It appears even that several of the refugees who had fled to France alter the sanguinary occurrences at Estclla had been recalled, and had been reinstated in their respective ranks.

AFFAIRS OF THE EAST. ( From the Morning Post.) We have just received the printed copies of the correspondence relating to Afghanistan, presented to the. House of Commons, on the 29th nit. We cannot at this moment find room for copious extracts from these interesting papers; hut we think it right to bring under the immediate notice of the British public one or two passages which we find in the letters of Lord Auckland, and which are of an importance that cannot fail to be fully understood and duly appreciated without any obsertalions from us. His lordship, addressing the secret committee of the Court of Directors, and dating Simla, the 22d of May, 1838, concludes in these emphatic words " I beg leave to draw the attention of your committee to the unequivocal demonstrations therein noted, of the extent to which Ku.-sid is

jr«wvrMi« carrying her system of interference oil the very threshold of the British Indian possessions. " 1 need not repeat my anxiety, even though the rapid march ot events may oblige me to act without your instructions, to be favoured with a communication of your views upon the present crisis at lire earliest possible opportunity." And again, addressing the same body at the date of the 13th of August, 1838, the Governor General of indiu concludes as follow s : þÿ

n\v former dispatches, of the manifest designs of the Russian officers to extend the interference and authority of their country to the borders of India. Y'he opposition of the Russian Ambassador before Herat, by which the e dor is of Mr. M'Neill to arrange a peace upon just and reasonable terms, between the Shah and the besieged, were wholly frustrated, when they seemed on the point oi being effectual ; the aid given by the Hussion Ambassador to the siege by advance of money ; and still more, the employment of an officer of the mission to direct the works of siege, are facts which will have forcibly arrested the attention of your committee." From the New York Daily Express, May 1. tub FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF the inauguration of Washington. The semi-centennial celebration yesterday was one of the most interesting events of the kind that ever took place in this city. The Historical Society made every arrangement that could add interest to the occasion. No individual now living was so well fitted as Mr. Adams, on every account, to deliver an oration on a fiftieth anniversary of an event so interesting as that of tne father of his couutrv taking the oath of the first chief magistrate of this mighty empire; and well did the venerable ex President, John Quincy Adams, ledeem the high expectation. At 11 o'clock the doors of the East Middle Dutch Church were thrown open, and those who applied for tickets had admission. Every spot was soon filled to overflowing, except that reserved for the members. At tweive o'clock the procession entered, when Peter G Stuyvesant took the chair, supported by the venerable Col. John Trumbull, and Morgan Lewis, who were the companions of Washington. President Duer, Gen. Scott, and ali the most distinguished gentlemen of our city were present, as well as distinguished delegates from other cities, The following Ode was sung : ODE Great were the hearts, and strong the minds Of those w ho framed, in high debate, The immortal league of love that binds Our fair broad empire, state with state,
And ever hollowed be the hour, When, as the auspicious task was done, A nation's gift, the sword of power, Was given to Glory's unspoiled son.
That noble race is gone : the suns Of fifty years have risen and set ; The holv links those mighty ones Had forged and knit, arc brighter yet.
þÿWide as our own- free race increase þÿ Wide shall it stretcli the elastic chain, And bind, in everlasting peace, State alter state, a mighty train.

Government of Ireland. It would, we apprehended, be taking a narrow view of the question, to suppose that it will be confined to the government of Ireland. The policy pursued with respect to Ireland is no doubt the point now attacked by the Tories ; but the Duke of Wellington is too considerate a man to take the bold step of going to issue on the government of Ireland without being prepared to avail himself ot all possible means by which he can strengthen his own party and weaken that of his opponents. The question is now substantially that which has been impending ever since the Reform of Parliament, though both parties have shrunk from the issue. But now that the Duke of Wellington has made up his mind to hazard it, we must give him credit for so much prudence as to believe that the war of parties will extend to all accessible points The House of Lords have impeached the Irish policy of Ministers since 1835, and it is proposed that the House of Commons shall vote a direct approbation of that which has been so impeached. þÿ So far so good. But the vote of the House of Commons will be only the commencement of a warfare of principle þÿ namely, a warfare to determine whether the Government shall be conducted in accordance with the opinion of the nation, cr in accordance with oligarchy, to defeat whose pretensions the Reform Bill, received hy general acclamation, was proposed andcariied. that is Liberal in the nation ; for by the support of the people alone can they hope to come victorious out ol the struggle. Now therefore, is the time for Liberal Members to come to an understanding on certain main sent divided. Throughout the country points on which they are notoriously at there preis a lukewarmness on lilie part of Reformers, because the expectations they were led to entertain from the Reform Bill have been disappointed ; and in consequence of the repeated declarations of Ministers with respect to the quality of the Reform Bill, they are without hope of enjoying the benefits for the sake of which they hailed that measure, and were ready to make every sacrifice to insure its success. Those Members who represent Liberal constituene.es know but too well the reluctance of their constituents to continue to make the efforts which in former times they cheerfully made, in hopes ol gaining tor a Liberal policy the ascendancy to which it is entitled. To revive the enthusiasm of the people, by which alone be the House of Lords can conducted collision with the to a successful issue, Ministers must make up their minds to abandon their negative policy, and to identify themselves with the whole Liberal party, by exerting themselves to remove admitted abuses, and to effect these changes in our institutions which experience, the best teacher, has proved to ho necessary, in oidcr | to allow a truly Liberal policy to he succcsii fully carried out .--Chronicle.

VALUABLE PROPERTY OF SILK. Dr. Adam Neale in his travels through Germany, Poland, Moldavia, and Turkey, published in 1818. records an extraordinary instance of the efficacy of silk in repelling a musket-shot, in a case which came under his own observation in Spain. þÿ A very promising young officer of engineers," says this writer,' þÿ with whom 1 lived in habits of the greatest intimacy and friendship, while employed in repairing the brut-

ches of Ciudad Rodrigo, consulted me respecting an obstinate headache and giddiness, which I found was principally occasioned by his wearing a stiff black leather stock. I earnestly recommended him to lay it aside, which he rather tenaciously declined ; when as a further inducement, 1 told him that in the event of his substituting a black silk liandkerchief, it might one day preserve his life, as silk would certainly turn a ball which might penetrate leather. At length he complied, and, as 1 had predicted, his headache left him. þÿ We soon alter separated; he going to the light division, and my station being with that of Lord Hill. The campaign commenced and in a few weeks 1 learned with the greatclaimed protection in case the federal army ! est grief, that my gallant friend had fallen at the head of the first storming party at St. We give the above news as we receive it I Sebastian. 1 was then stationed at Reynoza, many leagues distant. As 1 believed him dead, my surprise and joy were great on receiving a letter from him a few weeks afterwards, acquainting me, that wtien on the very glacis, he had been wounded with a musket ball by a man on the walls. He instantly fell covered with blood, which streamed in profusion from his mouth and nostrils; one of his own corps dragged him immediately into the trenches. He was carried to his quarters, and his wound, on examination, was pronounced mortal ; the ball not having been, found, was supposed to have lodged in the vertibiae ol the neck. He lived, however,

for three days, and no bad svmntoms comintr on, the surgeons began to doubt the accuracy of their opinions. The sapper who saw him fail was examined, to ascertain whether he had seen the bullet, which he instantly produced from fiis þÿw aistcoat pocket, saying, that untying Mr. þÿReid handkerchief, s he found part of it carried into the wound, and using a little force in withdrawing it, the bali came out with it; not a single thread of the silk handkerchief having given way, as appeared on examination. þÿ St. Thomas Times.

This invaluable collection of papers on the qualities and uses of salt, has nmv been long ® # enough in our hands to enable us to form an Nothing." he I opinion of its merits ; and certainly a more useful and universally beneficial document I has never been ordered by either House of Congress to lie printed. The subject is anaand so judiciously, that science and practice go hand in hand, and the most eminent chemist and the plainest farmer arrive at the same results. Salt itself is shown to be of verv different qualities, and adapted to very different purposes, ns being made either by boiling, or bv solar evaporation, or by crushing the mineral, or rock salt. Of these three kinds, that made by boiling is always impure, and is totally unfit for curing fish or provisions for long keeping, or for a Southern market, or for preserving Imiter. The crushed rock salt will do for curing fish, and is so used in England, but the solar made salt is the only pure and perfect salt, to be relied upon in all the great purposes to which salt is indispensable. I he reading of these papers will astonish people, in showing them the difference in the qualities of the three kinds of salt ; and all j will he gratified to sec that the best is both the cheapest and most abundant, and only J

ATS® wants fair play þÿ that is to sav," no tax and no monopoly þÿ to be produced in the amplest quantity tout the human race can require, ibis, of course, is the sun made salt, the quantity of which is only limitable by the limitations which the Deity lias placed on sunshine and sea water. The next best is the rock, or mineral salt, of Cheshire, in England ; and the quantity of this, also, is exceedingly þÿgreat If the duty was þÿoff (for even rock salt bears a duty of fifteen per cent, ad þÿvalorem) if this duty was off', this rock salt, either in masses or crushed, would come to the United States in vast quantities as ballast, and would be far better, and considerably cheaper, than the light blown salt which now comes from Liverpool. The dearest and worst salt is that made by boiling a process which prevents crystalization and the separation of impurities, and retains foreign and poisonous ingredients in the salt, and this in spite of all that the manufacturer can do to prevent it. But it is also shown that salt making, like every thing else, is subject to adulteration from practices to hasten its formation or improve its appearance ; and that lime is one of the deleterious ingredients used for this purpose, and greatly to the injury of the salt. VVe have seen a report from the superintendent of the New York salt works, denouncing this practice showing it was greatly practised, & that it was impossible to prevent it, as the boilers could always find their opportunity to throw lime

into the kettles. Such is the difference between sun made and boiled salt, that the latter weighs only about fifty pounds a bushel, while the former weighs eighty four pounds to the bushel ! Still more ample, scientific, and practical are those papers on the uses of salt. J hey present the great point of the uses of salt under three general divisions, to wit agriculture, manufactures, and the fishcrii s. Jn agriculture its uses are shown in promoting the health of every living animal; also, in improving the food that is taken by man or beast; also, in protecting seed grains fioni worms ; and in fertilizing the earth itself. Jn manufactures it is shown that there above filty varieties of productions in which salt is necessary, and is used either in its proper state, or as a chemical preparation. In þÿthe fisheries it is shown that boiled salt, except for the mere purpose of striking, as it is called, is no hotter than poison ; and that rock salt, crushed, or sun made salt, is absolutely indispensable to that great branch of business. I o the farmer, the manufacturer, and the fisherman, the information contained in these papers will he invaluable. The ellbct of their publication in England was electric. It caused the duty on foieign salt, and the excise on domestic stilt, to be immediately abolished, and it caused salt to be resorted to as one ol the principal means of improving the stock of Great Britain. It is unfortunate for the peace and commerce of this frontier that a portion of the Canadian people, and especially of the militia, act in concert with the Canadian refugees in their unhallowed effort to embroil two great and kindred nations in war. It is also to be regretted that this coincidence of purpose is encouraged by the general tone of the Canadian press, while the government of Toronto is acting, as may be seen by the correspondence in another column of this paper, in good faith and harmony with the mutual efforts of the British and American governments for the preservation of peace between the two countries. The Oswego editor is undoubtedly right in signalizing the Canadian militia, and some of the Canadian papers, as the perpetrators and instigators of these aggressions. The Coburgh Star and Toronto Patriot are unremitting in their endeavors to excite and keep up a spirit of hostility, in the minds of the Canadians, against the people of the United States þÿ principally, no doubt, in the vain and wicked hope of ultimately embroiling Great Britain and the United States in war. Sir George Arthur, we are confident, regards this spirit, and the acts to which it leads, with displeasure and regret ; but as was the case with our authorities, during the reign of" sympathy," he finds it easier to condemn and discountenance than to prevent, even with the strong military force at his command. It wiil be long, we fear, before we shall see the end of all the mischief that had its origin in the follv

and rashness of Sir Francis Head. STEAMBOAT GLASGOW. We find in the St. Louis Bulletin of the 26th April the following particulars of the destruction by fire of the steamboat William Glasgow. The Win. Glasgow. Captain Littleton, on her passage from Pittsburgh to this port, while in the Mississippe about 15 miles frotn the mouth of the Ohio, on Tuesday last took fire in the hold, and was consumed to the water's edge Such was the rapid progress of the flames, that nothing was saved, but a trifling amount of baggage by a few of the passengers and the books of the clerk's office. There was on board, at the time, upward# of a hundred passengers, consisting chiefly of emigrants, destined for Illinois and Missouri. Many of these emigrants had with them considerable sums of money in specie þÿ most of which was lost. One person lost in specie 3500 ; and the whole amount is conjectured to he not less than 15.000, besides furniture and other property. In truth many families are literally beggared. The steamer North Star þÿ which arrived here this morning, bringing the above intelligence þÿ succeeded, at great risk to itself, in rescuing a number from the burning wreck, and bro't to this place about one half of the passengers, some of whom are in a very destitute and pitiable condition. The Glasgow had on board two hogsheads and some kegs of powder, which fortunately did not explode, until the persons on board had made their escape. The confusion and trepidation of thejpassengers no doubt in this case as in all similar ones occasioned a needless abandonment of

þÿproperty and, we are pained to add þÿ the loss of one, if not two lives A German named Henry Brink, in the desperation of the moment leaped into the water and perished ; leaving a widow and two children. The captain and a portion of the passengers remained behind; without, however, the faintest prospect of recovering any thing, as the fire and explosion have completely annihilated both boat and cargo.

EXPRESS FROM PARIS. The Times Office, 3 o'clock a. m. The Paris pap'-rs of Monday have reached us l\v our usual express. Their contents are not, however, of importance. We have already said, that no Ministry could he formed until after the discussion of M. Maugnin's motion fixed for this day, and have only now to repeat that assurance. Various reports were circulated on Sunday evening respecting the formation of a Ministry, which was conceived by manv to he fast approaching to a conclusion. Others, usually well informed, discredited the statement. The Constituhinnel says, that the King had, in presence of a number of deputies who dined at the chateau, manifested no less surprise than the Chamber at the declaration ol M. Oirod dc I' \ in. Late in the evening Marshal Soult waited on His Majesty, but the friends of the Marshal knew nothing of the reported ariangernents, and even asserted that he had not resumed the powers which he returned the King after the failure of his attempt to construct a Cabinet. A letter dated Dresden, of the 29th ultimo, and published in the same journal, stales that Carlsbad will be this summer the seat of an absolutist congress, in which Austria is to he represented by Prince Metternich, Russia bv General Count de Witt, and Prussia by Baron Weither. The sovereigns of Germany, and

The exiled Royal Family of France had engaged an hotel in Carlsbad for the summer. þÿ Prince Wasa of Sweden would likewise spend tiie watering season at that residence. Advices from Berlin of the 27th ult. state that immediately upon being informed of the conclusion ot the treaty between Belgium and Holland, orders were forwarded by the Prussian Government to the Commanders of the 7th and 8th corps of the army, to disband the reserves, and place those corps on the peace footing. From the Courier de la Martinique, May 28. A spell of drought lias reigned in this colony for a considerable time. The temperature since the month of November seems to have undergone a total change. Instead of easterly, or north easterly winds which regularly prevailed at this period to the first of Julv, purifying and refreshing the ear, we have onlv experienced winds from the south southeast and south-west except during a verv few days. These burning winds, combined with the excessive heat and the drought, have been the principal cause of the sickness which lias ravaged the colony, especially since the 11th ol January. All the savannas are burnt up as if fire had passed through them. The earth shows large fissures every where, and in several places it lias fallen in. On Friday last a large portion oi a hill situated between St. Pierre and Carbct at Anse Tlmrin. slided into the sea which it displaced upwards of a hundred feet and formed a new promontory. Fortunately there are no victims to be regretted. Vegetation has been entirely arrested, and the crop of the next y ear must sutler considerably. The canes planted in last October, November and December have been checked by the dry weather, and many have perished altogether ; the Collee plantations have also suffered greatly, so that the future presents the most gloomy prospects. Constancy in Love is certainly not of every day's occurrence, but when it does occur, it has its advantages. It generates whatever is liberal and refined ; it purilies all that is gross: ii spurns all meanness; creates a no. bleiiess of sentiment, and equals in Ins mind a beggar with a prince, /'lie denizens of the world indeed whether votaries of ambition, of wealth, or of sensual pleasure, are not aole easily to understand the all absorbing power of a pure love or passion, when ii lias once taken possession of a sensitive mind. T hey know not of liovv little worth all other objects, all other things seem in comparison : how totally it sullices of itself for all mental, we had almost said all bodily food ; how entirely it can supply happiness, from mere meditation oil the beloved image. Hopelessness itself, as to the future, cannot deprive such a mind of the treasures of the past ; for the heart dwells upon what bus been with sometimes even more vivid feeling than upon what is. In this, even a despairing lover, penetrated by the recollection ot what he has enjoyed, though lost, may be compared lo a bereaved parent or husband, whose very agony is often soothed by remembrances, which might to some, be thought to increase it.
